videoIdeas.title: The room nobody lets you into
videoIdeas.hook: Nobody tells you the hardest part of leadership is just being allowed in the room.
videoIdeas.rationale: My top post ever ('Might not be the fastest in the room. But I am in the room') hit 2640 views because that line resonated. Lean into the same theme — presence over perfection — but build it into a full leadership lesson instead of a one-liner caption.
videoIdeas.script:
Nobody tells you the hardest part of leadership is just being allowed in the room.

Everyone obsesses over being the smartest, the fastest, the most qualified. But qualifications don't get you a seat. Showing up, consistently, when nobody's clapping — that gets you a seat.

I'm not the fastest in the room. I know that. But I'm in the room. And being in the room means I get to learn from the people who are faster, sharper, further ahead. You can't do that from the outside looking in.

So stop waiting until you're 'ready.' Ready is a myth. Get in the room half-finished and let the room finish you.

visuals.setting: Walking into a building or up a staircase, smart-casual, natural daylight. Mid-stride energy, handheld, slightly moving camera to match the 'in the room' motion.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'I'm not the fastest in the room.' as you push open a door and walk through — the door opening is the visual beat.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-walk, no intro, straight into the line
Freeze-frame on you stepping through a doorway with text punchline 'But I'm in it.'
Split screen: empty chair vs you sitting down in it

videoIdeas.title: Your voice shakes because you care
videoIdeas.hook: If your voice shakes when you speak in public — good. That's not weakness.
videoIdeas.rationale: Public speaking is one of my three pillars but barely shows up in my recent posts — clear content gap. Reframing nerves is a high-saves, relatable angle, similar to how doctordaanish and lifeofdinoo win with reframe content ('you can pray and still need help').
videoIdeas.script:
If your voice shakes when you speak in public — good. That's not weakness, that's your body telling you this matters to you.

The mistake is thinking confident speakers don't feel it. They feel everything. They've just stopped treating the shake as a signal to stop.

Here's the switch: you're not nervous, you're ready. Same racing heart, same dry mouth — different label. Your body can't tell the difference, so you decide what it means.

Next time you stand up and your hands go cold, don't apologise for it. Speak through it. The shake fades the moment you stop fighting it and start saying something true.

visuals.setting: Standing, mid-shot, plain background or in front of a small audience setup. Calm, grounded energy — deliberately still to contrast the topic of shaking.
visuals.visualHook: Hold your hand up to camera in the first second, slightly trembling, with on-screen text 'This is good actually.'
otherHookIdeas: Cold open on a close-up of a shaking hand gripping a mic
Pattern interrupt: start whispering then cut to full volume on 'Good.'
On-screen text countdown '3…2…1…' before you 'go on stage'

videoIdeas.title: Andalusia wasn't built by comfortable men
videoIdeas.hook: In 711 AD a man burned his own ships so his army couldn't retreat. Think about the leadership in that.
videoIdeas.rationale: My Tariq bin Ziyad post pulled 1640 views — Islamic history clearly works for my audience, but that caption got 0 comments because it was pure text with no takeaway. Repackage the same story as a leadership lesson with a clear point to drive discussion.
videoIdeas.script:
In 711 AD a man burned his own ships so his army couldn't retreat. Think about the leadership in that.

Tariq bin Ziyad crossed into Spain, lands on the shore, and orders the boats behind him set on fire. His men are terrified. His response: the enemy is in front of you, the sea is behind you, there is nowhere to run but forward.

That's not recklessness. That's removing the option of quitting. Most people fail not because they can't win, but because they left themselves an exit the whole time.

Leadership isn't always a speech. Sometimes it's burning the thing your people are secretly planning to run back to. What's your exit? And what would change if you took it off the table?

visuals.setting: Seated or standing, warm lighting, calm serious delivery. Could overlay simple historical imagery/maps as B-roll, but your face should carry it.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'He burned his own ships.' over a shot of you lighting or holding a flame/match — physical prop for the ships metaphor.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open on a map of Gibraltar with the date 711 AD stamped on
Pattern interrupt: 'This is the most underrated leadership move in history.'
End-card question on screen 'What's your exit?' to drive comments

videoIdeas.title: Burnout isn't a hustle problem
videoIdeas.hook: Burnout isn't what happens when you work too hard. It's what happens when you work hard at the wrong things.
videoIdeas.rationale: My Sabr/burnout post got 701 views and real engagement — burnout is clearly on my audience's mind, and doctordaanish's journaling/brain content proves 'fix your mind' topics are peaking right now. Give it a sharper reframe than the app promo version.
videoIdeas.script:
Burnout isn't what happens when you work too hard. It's what happens when you work hard at the wrong things.

You can study for twelve hours and feel fine if it means something to you. You can work two hours on something you resent and feel completely drained. The tiredness isn't about the hours. It's about the meaning.

So before you book another holiday to 'recover,' ask the harder question: are you exhausted, or are you just doing work you don't believe in?

Rest fixes tired. It doesn't fix misaligned. If you come back from a week off and dread Monday the exact same way — that's not burnout. That's a signal. Listen to it.

visuals.setting: Low-key, early morning or late night energy — desk, dim lamp, tired-but-honest tone. Dressed down. Direct to camera, quieter delivery.
visuals.visualHook: Shot of you closing a laptop slowly with on-screen text 'Rest won't fix this.'
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-sigh rubbing your eyes at a desk
On-screen text punchline reveal: 'you're not tired, you're misaligned'
Pattern interrupt: pour out a coffee into the sink as you say the hook

videoIdeas.title: The park at night taught me something
videoIdeas.hook: I said I'd never run through a park at night again. Then I realised that fear was running my whole life.
videoIdeas.rationale: My park-at-night running video hit 1537 views on a light, funny caption. Build on that momentum and that same relatable 'me running' format my audience already responds to — but turn the joke into a sharper mindset point to deepen it.
videoIdeas.script:
I said I'd never run through a park at night again. Then I realised that fear was running my whole life.

It's easy to laugh it off. Dark park, weird noises, you leg it home. Funny. But then I started counting all the other things I avoid because of a version of that same feeling. The conversation I don't start. The idea I don't pitch. The gym at peak hours.

Fear's job is to keep you alive. It is terrible at keeping you growing. Those are two different jobs.

I'm not telling you to be reckless. I'm telling you to notice how often 'I don't feel like it' is actually 'I'm scared and dressing it up.' Name it honestly and half its power is gone.

visuals.setting: Outdoors, evening, running gear — same world as the post that worked. Start light and slightly comedic, shift to serious as the point lands.
visuals.visualHook: Cold open mid-run, out of breath, glancing over your shoulder with on-screen text 'never again 😭' — then record-scratch into the real point.
otherHookIdeas: Pattern interrupt: comedic jump/flinch then straight to camera
On-screen text transition 'but here's what it actually taught me'
Freeze on your face mid-run with the reframe line as text

videoIdeas.title: How to actually connect in a room of strangers
videoIdeas.hook: Stop asking people 'so what do you do.' It's the fastest way to be forgotten.
videoIdeas.rationale: birdtart01's networking question video did 2.1M views — practical networking/communication content is the single biggest-performing format across my competitor set, and it sits squarely in my public speaking pillar, which I'm currently neglecting. Direct, saveable, blunt format.
videoIdeas.script:
Stop asking people 'so what do you do.' It's the fastest way to be forgotten.

Everyone asks it, so everyone's answer is on autopilot. You get a job title, they get a job title, nobody remembers a thing.

Try this instead. 'What's been taking up most of your head space lately?' Now they have to actually think, and they'll tell you what they care about, not what's on their LinkedIn.

Or: 'What brought you here tonight, specifically?' The word 'specifically' does the work — it stops the generic answer.

Connection isn't about being interesting. It's about asking the question nobody else bothered to ask. Do that once and you're the person they remember from the whole room.

visuals.setting: Smart-casual, upbeat energy, could be in a social/event-style setting or clean background. Punchy, quick cuts between each question.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'STOP asking this →' with a big crossed-out 'so what do you do?' in the first second.
otherHookIdeas: Yellow-font style text overlay for each question (format birdtart01 wins with)
Cold open mid-handshake with text 'you already lost them'
Numbered on-screen list that builds as you speak for high saves

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is your best post for a reason — 2640 views, 121 likes, 11 comments. The caption 'Might not be the fastest in the room. But I am in the room' is pure you: blunt, rhythmic, a reframe anyone can apply to themselves. It's personal (running) but the lesson is universal, which is why it travelled.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: You left the insight on the table. The caption nails the hook but gives no follow-through — turn that line into a pinned series. Add a one-line CTA ('Where are you still waiting to be ready?') to convert those 121 likes into more than 11 comments. The reframe deserves a full video, not just a caption.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 1640 views and the Islamic history angle clearly lands with your audience — this is a lane your competitors aren't fully occupying. The specificity (711 AD, Tariq bin Ziyad, names and dates) gives it authority and makes it feel researched, not recycled.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Zero comments despite strong views means it informed but didn't provoke. The caption reads like a history lesson with no takeaway for the viewer's own life. End with a leadership question or a 'what would you have done' to pull people into the comments. Also the caption is cut off mid-sentence — tighten it so the payoff isn't lost.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 1537 views on a light, honest, funny caption — 'Never running through a park at night ever again 😭' is relatable and human, and it got 5 comments because it invited people to share their own version. This shows your audience likes seeing the real you, not just the teacher you.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: It's your second-best performer but it's pure entertainment with no depth hook to make people follow. You don't need to kill the humour — just add one line that turns the joke into an idea, so people save it and not just chuckle. The relatable-personal format is a goldmine; pair it with a point.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 701 views and real engagement on a genuinely useful topic. Burnout is clearly resonating, and opening with 'whether you're a medical student or not' smartly widens the audience beyond one niche. The emojis and plain language keep it approachable.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: This reads like an ad for Sabr more than your take on burnout, and the drop in performance shows it — people scroll past promo. Lead with your own blunt insight on burnout first, earn the attention, then mention the app. Also the caption is cut off; don't bury the hook behind product copy.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 289 likes — your highest like count here — proves your audience shows up hard for justice and principle. The hadith framing ('change it with his hand, tongue, or heart') is exactly your voice: rooted, direct, no fluff. People respect that you took a stand with a name attached.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: It's a Sidecar (image carousel) with no views metric and only 1 comment — the format capped its reach. Your audience clearly cares about this, so deliver it as a video next time to tap the algorithm the way your Reels do. And a direct CTA ('tag someone who needs to hear this' or a specific action) would convert that passion into shares, not just likes.
